That said, while I expected favorable gameplay, I didn't expect the underlying story. I could tell that there was something going on within Quell and Reflect, but as everything finally came together in Memento, I couldn't help but feel sad as things finally made sense. With a man looking back on his life over the years and getting closure on his time, it helped me reflect on my own life and consider where I cam now. I certainly have many more years in my own life, but I sincerely do hope I can make the most of my time with my loved ones. Quell Memento is a mobile app that's been dumped on Steam as if it was a real PC game (it's not)... it's a cash grab from greedy mobile devs.  The game The game is a very simple pathing puzzle game.  You control a blue pixel blob.  You can move in any direction, but once you start moving, you don't stop until you hit a wall.  Basically this is the same game as the countless Russian "Chocolate Makes You Happy" ClickTeam Fusion asset flips infesting Steam.  It's also been copy + pasted a few times by the developers themselves (Quell, Quell Reflect, all the same game).  Asset flipping begins at home!

From a technical perspective, as a mobile app, this doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

The mobile app features somewhat lazy, simplistic 2D graphics, of the type you normally expect to see in low effort Flash/browser games and mobile apps.  Considering this is being evaluated as a PC game, having the graphics phoned in like this isn't going to result in a high quality, visually impressive game that PC gamers are used to seeing.

The developers didn't design the mobile app for modern gaming PCs, as such the display resolution caps out below 4K, despite 4K entering the mainstream in 2014.  The mobile app simply won't look right on modern gaming displays due to this failure on the part of the developers.

Because this is a mobile app, it carries a number of deliberate design deficiencies.  Compromises were made to cater to the iPhones that the mobile app was designed for.  These are unfortunate handicaps and limitations that PC gamers shouldn't be forced to accept, but it's evident that PC was an afterthought for the iPhone developers who are to blame for this.  The mobile app is deficient as a result of these choices, and would have been so much better without the handicaps that designing games for mobile phones forces upon a game.  Once more, mobile devs have made gaming worse for everyone.  I didn't spend thousands on building a gaming rig just so I could pretend it's an iPhone.

These technical defects push this mobile app below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

The poor quality of this mobile app is reflected by how many people spent time with it.  At the time of this review, SteamDB shows the all-time peak player number was only 9 players.  This is a remarkably low number, and now, the only player activity occurs once or twice a month, presumably someone loading it up to see what it is then quickly uninstalling it.  Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 50,000 games for gamers to choose from, the overwhelming lack of interest in this low quality mobile app is to be expected.

Quell Memento has the almost unethical price of around $4 USD (for a garbage mobile app!), 50C more than the dev gouges mobile peasants for, which is an appalling insult, it's also not worth it given the defects and shortcomings with the product, especially considering the sheer number of completely free, much higher quality games on Steam.

[i]Quell Memento[/i] is a puzzle game with narrative elements. Though the narrative portion of this game is pretty inconsequential, the puzzles themselves make a solid time. The game gets quite hard for the latter levels, but a comprehensive hint system balances things out for those who wish to utilize it. It even goes so far as to make the game too easy if abused, so it's up to the player to restrain themselves. Overall, this is a decent value for the price, especially if on sale.

[i]Quell Memento[/i]'s 150+ levels feature blue balls in mazes. The goal is to either collect all the grey balls or light up all level tiles. The game is divided into nine chapters of sixteen levels; each chapter introduces new mechanics until the final few chapters put them together for the toughest challenge. Meanwhile, chapters are themed around the life and death of one man, with a narrator interspersing chapters with cryptic commentary. The game's soundtrack conveys a sophisticated, melancholy tone.

The puzzles are designed well. The game has a rather steep difficulty curve, with roughly the first third of the game being nearly trivial and the final few chapters immensely difficult. Puzzles contain secret gems (and perhaps other things) hidden beneath level tiles that need to be smashed to retrieve them; it's a small pleasure to be able to bash around looking for each secret. Messing around with the dynamic new mechanics is also somewhat fun, though ultimately players will be drawn to not mess around too much as the focus will be on finishing each level with the fewest moves.

The game offers a robust hint system to balance the difficulty - going so far as to overcompensate. Each guided level solution costs two coins, while finishing a level perfectly earns one coin. Since you keep the coin you get when helped by a hint, each hint costs a net one coin. With each hint balanced by each hint-free perfect level, a player can effectively only have to play half of the game, which can easily be done for the early chapters and the introductory levels for each new gimmick. Of course there are some other uses for coins, so half the game likely won't be trivialized for most, but typically there's more restraint or cost associated with level skips than this. This likely accounts for why Steam says over one third of players have beaten every level perfectly.

[i]Quell Memento[/i] otherwise doesn't have much else - not like it needs anything. The narrative aspects are fairly underwhelming given the disjointed narration and the lack of connection to the cycle of life aside from the level titles. It should also be noted that this is clearly a mobile port, but it is an inoffensive port job. The UI is only stands out on the Pause Menu, and the controller support is smooth and responsive. Otherwise, since the puzzles are good, the game is good.

The roughly 4-5 hours of this game should satisfy less skilled players who can lean on the expansive hint system, as well as those seeking a pure challenge to perfect and find every level's bonus. Though the advertised narrative angle isn't very impactful, the puzzles in this one should quell any doubt's about this title's quality. [i]Quell Memento[/i] gets a B+.

独特的叙事方式需要玩家互动而又不那么繁琐，关卡内容与故事情节相互对应，加上本系列一贯的高质量音乐和美术风格，使整个故事情节引人入胜，让玩家沉浸在叙事者的回忆之中．人生的结束就像是标题界面时玻璃的破碎，而我们正是通过这些记忆碎片，拼凑还原出叙事者的一生．
另外，Quell系列是从移动端上移植过来的，但是几乎找不到移植的痕迹，加上游戏本身的内容和合理的难度梯度，可以说是解谜游戏中无可挑剔的上乘之作．

Катаем шары и собираем жемчужины. Звучит очень примитивно,правда?
Главная задача, собрать жемчужины или заставить светится кристаллы за минимальное количество движений. 

Плюсики:
-Сюжет. Сам был приятно удивлён. В первой части его в помине не было и он в такой игре нафиг не нужон, но здесь он органично встраивается в игру. Он достаточно прост, но трогателен. Историю повествует о старике, который вспоминает своё прошлое и рефлексирует над этим.
-Музыка. Хороша чертовка. Околоклассическая музыка на пианино на протяжении всей игры создаёт меланхоличную атмосферу.
-Разнообразие. В отличие от первой части, здесь много всяких свистелок и перделок. Авторы высосали из примитивной идеи абсолютно всё. Или нет?*агрессивно поглядывает на Quell Reflect*

Минусик:
- Затянутость. Первые часа три я кайфовал, а потом... одно и тоже, одно и тоже. Понемногу я начинал скучать и заканчивал игру со скрипом

一款解谜游戏
控制小水滴移动，通过尽量少的步数拾取场景中的所有小球
难点在于小球并不是一格格移动，而是必须要碰到障碍物才能停止
应该是系列游戏的第三部，内容上比前2部更丰富，比如一些特殊触发效果的陷阱、多水滴合作等等
而且除了之前一样每关都有的隐藏宝石外，还多了一些隐藏关卡，变相的等于增加了关卡数量
总体来说是一款不错值得一玩的小游戏
